q: 301. In a stair the most suitable position to provide winders is ..........
explain: Winders are tapered steps used to change the direction of a stair without a landing. They are safest and most commonly placed at the start (bottom) of a flight.

q: 302. The height of hand railing above the tread should be generally between ..........
explain: For ergonomic comfort and safety, handrails are typically fixed at a height of 750 mm to 800 mm (75-80 cm) above the line of nosing.

q: 303. The narrow strips of wood or bands of plaster laid on the floor at intervals to act as guides for bringing the whole of the true and even surface are termed as ..........
explain: Screeds are narrow strips laid on a floor to act as gauges or guides for maintaining an even thickness and level surface of the concrete or mortar.

q: 304. The cheapest floor which remains warm in winter and cool in summer is ..........
explain: Mud flooring is inexpensive and possesses excellent thermal insulation properties, naturally regulating temperature throughout the seasons.

q: 305. The lowest part of a structure which transmits the load to the soil is known as ..........
explain: The foundation is the sub-structure that transfers the building weight to the underlying soil or rock.

q: 306. The foundation in a building is provided to ..........
options: distribute the load over a large area
increase overall stability of the structure
transmit load to the bearing surface(sub soil) at a uniform rate
explain: Foundations ensure stability, prevent unequal settlement, and distribute heavy loads over a wider area to avoid soil failure.

q: 307. The failure of foundation of a building is due to ..........
options: lateral escape of the supporting material
explain: Foundations fail when soil shifts laterally, moisture changes cause volume shifts (like in clay), or when one part of the building settles more than another.

q: 308. The ability of sub-soil to support the load of the structure without yielding is known as ..........
explain: Bearing capacity (or value/power) refers to the soil's resistance to compression and shear failure under structural loads.

q: 309. The bearing capacity of soils can be improved by ..........
options: ramming the granular material like crushed stone in the soil
explain: Improving bearing capacity involves increasing depth to reach firmer strata, removing excess water, or mechanically compacting the soil.

q: 310. The maximum bearing capacity of soil is that of ..........
explain: Igneous and hard rocks have the highest safe bearing capacity, often exceeding 3000-4000 kN/m².

q: 311. When the walls are subjected to heavy loading and the bearing capacity of the soil is very low, the wall is constructed on ..........
explain: R.C.C. footings are used for heavy loads on weak soil because reinforcement allows the footing to resist tension and distribute weight more effectively.

q: 312. When heavy structural loads from columns are required to be transferred to a soil of low bearing capacity, the most economical foundation is ..........
explain: Grillage foundations (using steel beams or timber) are economical for spreading heavy column loads over a wide area without deep excavation.

q: 313. In order to protect the beam against corrosion, a minimum cover of ........ is kept on the outer sides of the external beams as well as above the upper flange of the top tier.
explain: In grillage foundations, steel beams are encased in concrete with at least 100 mm cover to protect against moisture and corrosion.

q: 314. In masonry construction, excessive tension is not permissible and hence in order that the supporting area is fully in compression, the width of footing is so adopted that the centre of gravity of the load falls ..........
options: within the middle third of base
within the middle fifth of base
explain: To avoid tension at the base of a masonry footing, the eccentricity of the load must be limited so the resultant force stays within the middle third.

q: 315. In made-up ground having a low value of its bearing power, heavy concentrated structural loads are generally supported by providing ..........
explain: Raft (mat) foundations are best for 'made-up' or soft ground as they bridge over weak spots and prevent differential settlement.

q: 316. Which of the following foundation is used for weaker soil?
explain: While all spread footings help, raft foundations are specifically designed to handle the most challenging weak soil conditions.

q: 317. The raft foundations are generally used when the required area of footing is ........ the total area of the surface.
explain: Standard practice dictates that if the total area of individual footings exceeds 50% (one-half) of the building area, a raft is used.

q: 318. When two or more footings are connected by a beam, it is called ..........
explain: A strap footing consists of two isolated footings joined by a structural 'strap' beam to transfer eccentric loads.

q: 319. A foundation consisting of thick reinforced concrete slab covering the entire area of the bottom of the structure, is known as ..........
explain: A raft or mat foundation is a continuous slab that supports all the columns and walls of a structure.

q: 320. A black cotton soil is unsuitable for foundations because it ..........
options: undergoes volumetric changes with the change of atmospheric conditions
explain: Black cotton soil contains montmorillonite clay which expands and contracts violently with moisture changes, causing structures to crack.

q: 321. When the heavy structure is to be constructed in sandy soil, the foundation used is ..........
explain: Depending on the density and depth of the sand, piers, straps, or rafts may be used to provide adequate bearing.

q: 322. Pile foundation is generally used when the soil is ..........
explain: Piles are deep foundations used when surface soil is weak, water-logged, or unreliable, transferring loads to deeper, firmer strata.

q: 323. The type of foundation most suitable for bridges is ..........
explain: Pier foundations are commonly used for bridge structures to transfer heavy loads through water or soft soil to hard rock.

q: 324. A combined footing is commonly used ..........
options: when two columns are spaced close to each other
when two columns are spaced far apart
explain: When columns are so close that their individual footings would overlap, they are merged into a single combined footing.

q: 325. The piles which do not support the load by themselves, but act as a medium to transmit the load from the foundation to the resisting sub-stratum, are known as ..........
explain: End-bearing piles act like columns, transmitting the load through their tips directly to a hard-resisting layer.

q: 326. The piles which are driven in the type of soil whose strength does not increase with depth or where the rate of increase in strength with depth is very slow, are known as ..........
explain: Friction piles derive their carrying capacity from the skin friction between the pile surface and the surrounding soil along the entire length of the pile.

q: 327. In combined footing ..........
options: center of gravity of the column loads must coincide with the center of gravity of the footing
explain: For uniform pressure distribution in a combined footing, the geometric center (C.G.) of the footing must coincide with the resultant C.G. of the loads from both columns.

q: 328. Batter piles are ..........
options: used to function as retaining walls
used to protect concrete deck or other water front structures from the abrasion or impact
driven at an inclination to resist large horizontal inclined forces
driven in granular soil with the aim of increasing the bearing capacity of the soil
explain: Batter piles (or raking piles) are driven at an angle to the vertical to resist lateral loads, such as wind or water pressure.

q: 329. Fender piles are ..........
options: used to function as retaining walls
used to protect concrete deck or other water front structures from the abrasion or impact
driven at an inclination to resist large horizontal inclined forces
driven in granular soil with the aim of increasing the bearing capacity of the soil
explain: Fender piles are provided in waterfront structures to absorb the impact of berthing ships and protect the main structure from damage.

q: 330. The best spacing of timber piles from center to center is ..........
explain: A spacing of 900 mm (or 3 times the diameter) is generally recommended for timber piles to ensure proper group action and soil stability.

q: 331. The maximum load on the wooden pile should not exceed ..........
explain: Due to the natural strength limits of timber, the safe working load for a standard wooden pile is usually restricted to 200 kN (approx. 20 tons).

q: 332. Pre-cast concrete piles are usually ..........
options: plain, reinforced concrete or pre-stressed concrete
explain: Pre-cast piles must withstand lifting and driving stresses, which require them to be either reinforced (RCC) or pre-stressed concrete.

q: 333. The length of pre-cast concrete piles varies from ..........
explain: Pre-cast piles are manufactured in lengths up to 30 meters, though longer ones are difficult to transport and handle without specialized equipment.

q: 334. Cast-in-situ piles is ..........
options: are cast in position inside the ground
need not be reinforced in ordinary cases
are not subjected to handling or driving stresses
explain: Since they are formed in the ground, cast-in-situ piles avoid the stresses of transport and driving, allowing for more flexible design.

q: 335. A type of cast-in-situ pile suited for places where the ground is soft and offers little resistance to the flow of concrete, is ..........
explain: Vibro-piles use a vibrating casing that compacts the soil and ensures a dense concrete column even in soft soil conditions.

q: 336. A type of cast-in-situ pile which has an enlarged base and a corrugated stem, is ..........
explain: Franki piles feature a 'mushroom' base formed by ramming dry concrete into the soil, significantly increasing the end-bearing area.

q: 337. The diameter of the drilled piles should not exceed ..........
explain: Standard drilled or bored piles for smaller structures typically range up to 600 mm in diameter.

q: 338. The pre-stressed concrete piles as compared to pre-cast and reinforced concrete piles ..........
explain: Pre-stressed piles are efficient because the high-strength steel and pre-compression allow for smaller sections with higher durability and load capacity.

options: cannot withstand large impact stress developed during hand driving
explain: H-piles (steel I-beams) are actually easy to store, handle, and can withstand extremely high driving stresses, making all the provided negative statements false.

q: 340. A steel pile which function more efficiently in soft clay or loose sand, is ..........
explain: The large helical blades of a screw pile provide significant uplift and bearing resistance in soft or loose soils.

q: 341. A screw pile consists of cast iron or steel shaft of external diameter varying from ..........
explain: The central shaft of a screw pile is typically between 150 mm and 300 mm, though the helix blade diameter is much larger.

q: 342. Sheet piles are made of ..........
explain: Sheet piles can be made of timber for light work, reinforced concrete for permanent structures, or steel for high-strength temporary or permanent shoring.

q: 343. The coefficient of friction between the concrete and soil is ..........
explain: The friction factor (tan δ) for concrete against average soil ranges from 0.30 to 0.35 for design calculations.

q: 344. When the pile is required to penetrate beds of hard soil or soft rock to reach its required depth, the best method of driving the pile is by ..........
explain: Boring (pre-drilling) removes the hard material that a standard hammer cannot penetrate, allowing the pile to reach the design depth.

q: 345. When the pile is driven by means of water jets, water is forced through the jet pipe under a pressure of ..........
explain: Jetting uses water pressure (0.7 to 1.75 MPa) to displace soil at the pile tip, facilitating easier penetration in sandy or gravelly soils.

q: 346. The center to center spacing of lateral reinforcement in pre-cast reinforced concrete piles should not exceed ........ the least width of the pile.
explain: To prevent buckling of the main bars and to resist driving shocks, the lateral ties are closely spaced at half the pile width.

q: 347. For the pre-cast reinforced concrete piles, the quality of concrete recommended is ..........
explain: M150 to M200 (approx. M15 to M20) is the minimum grade used to ensure the pile can handle the severe stresses of hammer impact.

q: 348. In the pre-cast reinforced concrete piles, the thickness of concrete covering the main bars should not be less than ..........
explain: A minimum clear cover of 40 mm is required for standard piles to protect the reinforcement from soil-based corrosion.

q: 349. The minimum of covering of the reinforcement for the pre-cast reinforced piles used in sea water, is ..........
explain: Due to the highly corrosive nature of chloride in seawater, the cover is increased to 75 mm to prevent the steel from rusting.

q: 350. A temporary structure constructed in a river for excluding water from a given site to enable the building operation to be performed on dry surface, is called ..........
explain: A cofferdam is a temporary enclosure pumped dry to allow construction work (like bridge piers) to take place below the water level.

q: 351. When the depth of water is from 4.5 to 6 m, the type of cofferdam used is ..........
explain: For depths between 4.5 and 6 meters, a double-walled cofferdam provides the necessary stability and water-tightness that simpler earthen or single-walled structures cannot.

q: 352. A watertight structure constructed in connection with excavations for foundations of bridges, piers etc., is known as ..........
explain: A caisson is a permanent, watertight retaining structure used for foundations of bridges and other heavy structures in water or wet ground.

q: 353. The minimum depth of foundation for the load bearing wall of a building is restricted to ..........
explain: In standard construction practice, the minimum depth for a load-bearing wall foundation is 900 mm to ensure it reaches below the zone of seasonal soil movement.

q: 354. In order that the wall may be stable, the lowermost course of the wall footing is made ........ the width of the wall.
explain: According to the rule of thumb for spread footings, the width of the base of the foundation should be twice the width of the wall.

q: 355. The dampness in a building is due to ..........
explain: Dampness is caused by multiple factors including capillary action from the ground, penetration of rain through walls/roofs, and poor material choices or workmanship.

q: 356. The dampness on roof may be due to ..........
explain: Roof dampness often stems from porous tiles/slabs, inadequate overlap of roofing sheets allowing wind-driven rain to enter, or leaking pipes.

q: 357. The most commonly used material for damp proofing is ..........
explain: Bitumen is the most widely used damp-proofing material due to its flexibility, water-repellent nature, and ease of application as a membrane or paint.

q: 358. In case of building without basement, the best position for damp-proof course (D.P.C.) lies at ..........
explain: Providing DPC at the plinth level effectively interrupts the capillary rise of water from the foundation into the superstructure walls.

q: 359. For D.P.C. at plinth level, the commonly adopted material is ..........
explain: Mastic asphalt is a semi-rigid material that is highly durable and completely impervious, making it ideal for plinth-level damp proofing.

q: 360. A semi-rigid material which forms an excellent impervious layer for damp-proofing, is called ..........
explain: Mastic asphalt is defined by its semi-rigid property and its ability to provide a seamless, waterproof barrier.

q: 361. The damp-proof course ..........
options: should be of good impervious material
explain: An effective DPC must be continuous to prevent any gaps for moisture, made of impervious material, and applied where moisture penetration is likely.

q: 362. The cavity wall is generally provided for ..........
explain: The air gap in a cavity wall acts as a barrier to moisture, heat transfer, and sound, significantly improving the building's internal environment.

q: 363. A flexible material used for D.P.C. is ..........
explain: Bitumen sheeting (bituminous felt) is a flexible membrane that can adapt to small structural movements without cracking.

q: 364. The construction of a temporary structure required to support an unsafe structure, is called ..........
explain: Shoring is the provision of temporary supports (shores) to provide lateral or vertical stability to an unsafe or damaged wall.

q: 365. A temporary rigid structure having platforms raised up as the building increases in height, is called ..........
explain: Scaffolding is a temporary framework used to provide a safe working platform for laborers and materials during construction or repair.

q: 366. The arrangement of supports provided underneath the existing structure without disturbing its stability, is known as ..........
explain: Underpinning is the process of strengthening or deepening the foundation of an existing structure.

q: 367. A raking shore is a system of ..........
options: giving temporary lateral support to an unsafe wall
providing temporary support to the party walls of two buildings where the intermediate building is to be pulled down and rebuilt
providing vertical support to walls and roofs, floors etc. when the lower part of a wall has to be removed for the purpose of providing an opening in the wall
explain: Raking shores consist of inclined timber members (rakers) used to provide lateral support to walls that are bulging or out of plumb.

q: 368. For a building on the side of a busy street where the ordinary scaffolding will obstruct the traffic on road, the type of scaffolding provided is ..........
explain: Needle scaffolding (cantilever scaffolding) is supported by 'needles' projecting from the wall, keeping the ground level clear for traffic.

q: 369. A horizontal layer of bricks laid in mortar is known as ..........
explain: In masonry, a course is a single continuous horizontal layer of bricks or stones.

q: 370. The brick laid with its length perpendicular to the face of the wall is called a ..........
explain: A header is a brick laid so that only its end (the smaller face) is visible on the surface of the wall.

q: 371. The brick laid with its length parallel to the face of the wall is called a ..........
explain: A stretcher is a brick laid so that its long face is parallel to the face of the wall.

q: 372. A system of providing temporary support to the party walls of two buildings when the intermediate building is to be pulled down and built, is called ..........
explain: Flying shores (horizontal shores) support two parallel walls across an open space without touching the ground.

q: 373. A brick which is cut in such a way that the width of its one end is half that of a full brick, is called ..........
explain: A king closer is formed by cutting a triangular corner of the brick such that the width of one end is half the width of the brick.

q: 374. A brick which is half as wide as a full brick, is called ..........
explain: A queen closer is obtained by cutting a brick lengthwise into two equal halves.

q: 375. Frog is defined as a ..........
options: depression on the top face of a brick
brick whose one end is cut splayed or mitred for the full width
brick used for the corner of a wall
explain: The frog is the indentation on the top face of a brick designed to hold mortar and create a mechanical key between courses.

q: 376. The most important purpose of a frog in a brick is to ..........
options: form keyed joint between brick and mortar
explain: By filling with mortar, the frog creates a strong 'key' that prevents the bricks from sliding relative to one another.

q: 377. In brick masonry, for good bonding ..........
options: all bricks need not be uniform in size
bats must be used in alternate courses only
vertical joints in alternate courses should fall in plumbs
cement mortar must have surkhi as additive
explain: Proper bonding requires that vertical joints are broken (staggered) so they do not form a continuous line of weakness through the wall.

q: 378. King closers are related to ..........
explain: King closers are specialized brick shapes used in brick masonry to facilitate the bonding pattern at corners or openings.

q: 379. Cornice is defined as a ..........
options: horizontal course of masonry projecting from the face of the wall
horizontal moulded projection near the top of a building
covering placed on the exposed top of an external wall
triangular shaped portion of masonry at the end of a sloped roof
explain: A cornice is a decorative and functional horizontal projection that finishes the top of a wall or building.

q: 380. Coping is defined as a ..........
options: horizontal course of masonry projecting from the face of the wall
horizontal moulded projection near the top of a building
covering placed on the exposed top of an external wall
triangular shaped portion of masonry at the end of a sloped roof
explain: Coping is a protective cap (usually stone or concrete) placed on top of a wall to shed water and prevent moisture from entering the masonry.

q: 381. A horizontal member of stone, concrete or wood provided to give support for the vertical member of a wooden window, is called ..........
explain: The sill is the horizontal bottom member of a window frame that sheds water away from the wall.

q: 382. The exposed vertical surface left on the sides of an opening after the door or window frame has been fitted in position, is called ..........
explain: The reveal is the part of the side of a window or door opening that is visible between the frame and the outer surface of the wall.

q: 383. A bat is the portion of a ..........
options: brick cut in such a manner that its one long face remains uncut
explain: A brick bat is a piece of brick that has been cut across its width, usually classified as half-bat or three-quarter bat.

q: 384. Hearting is the portion of a ..........
options: brick cut in such a manner that its one long face remains uncut
explain: In thick walls, hearting is the interior portion of the wall between the exterior facing and the interior backing.

q: 385. A course of stone provided immediately below a cornice, is called ..........
explain: In classical architecture and stone masonry, the frieze is the course located directly underneath the projecting cornice.

q: 386. A course of stone masonry provided immediately above the cornice, is called ..........
explain: A blocking course is a heavy course of stone laid over the cornice to add weight and stabilize the structure.

q: 387. The type of stone masonry commonly adopted in the construction of residential building is ..........
explain: Coursed rubble masonry is popular for residential work because it is stronger and more aesthetically pleasing than uncoursed types.

q: 388. In the first class coursed rubble masonry ..........
options: all the courses are of the same height
minimum height of the course is limit to 150 mm
the length of the quoin is generally kept 450 mm
explain: First-class coursed rubble requires uniform course heights and specific stone dimensions for maximum structural integrity.

q: 389. The type of masonry in which the stones of irregular size and shapes are used and there are no regular courses, is known as ..........
explain: Uncoursed rubble masonry is the most basic form, where stones are used as they come from the quarry with minimal dressing.

q: 390. In stretching bond ..........
options: all the bricks are laid as headers
all the bricks are laid as stretchers
the arrangement of bricks is similar to English bond
the bonding bricks are laid at any angle other than zero or ninety degrees
explain: Stretching bond consists entirely of stretchers and is used primarily for half-brick thick partition walls.

q: 391. A type of bond in which all the bricks are laid as headers on the faces of walls, is known as ..........
explain: Heading bond uses only headers and is useful for constructing curved walls or footings.

q: 392. A bond consisting of heading and stretching courses so arranged that one heading course comes after several stretching courses, is called ..........
explain: Facing bond is used when expensive facing bricks are used for the outer skin and cheaper bricks for the backing.

q: 393. A stretcher bond is usually used for ..........
explain: Since all bricks are laid lengthwise, a stretcher bond cannot provide a transverse bond, limiting it to half-brick (10cm) walls.

q: 394. The heading bond is usually used for ..........
explain: Heading bond is primarily used for full-width (one brick) walls where maximum strength across the wall is needed.

q: 395. The most commonly used bond for all wall thickness is ..........
explain: English bond is considered the strongest bond in brickwork and is the standard for most structural wall construction.

q: 396. Herring-bone bond is commonly used for ..........
explain: Herring-bone bond, where bricks are laid at 45 degrees, is highly decorative and provides excellent interlocking for floor pavings.

q: 397. The filling in cavities with cement slurry is known as ..........
explain: Grouting is the process of injecting or pouring a fluid cement mixture (slurry) into voids or cracks to fill them.

q: 398. In a raking bond ..........
options: the bricks are laid as headers
all the bricks are laid as stretchers
the arrangement of bricks is similar to English bond
the bonding bricks are laid at any angle other than zero or ninety degrees
explain: Raking bonds (like diagonal or herring-bone) involve laying bricks at an angle to increase longitudinal strength in thick walls.

q: 399. The arrangement of bricks is similar to English bond in ..........
explain: Dutch bond is a modified version of English bond that uses specialized patterns at the corners to avoid using too many closers.

q: 400. A wall built to resist the pressure of earth filling, is known as ..........
explain: A retaining wall is a structural wall designed to hold back soil or other materials at a slope steeper than the natural angle of repose.
